questions.q: By contrast, $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges. Compare the graphs of $y=\frac{1}{x}$ and $y=\frac{1}{x^2}$ on $[1,10]$ and explain why $\frac{1}{x}$ decays too slowly for the area to stay finite.
questions.target: Visualizing convergence: area under the curve
questions.answer: Both curves decrease, but $\frac{1}{x}$ stays larger than $\frac{1}{x^2}$ for all $x>1$ (e.g. at $x=10$: $0.1$ vs $0.01$). This slower decay means the accumulated area under $\frac{1}{x}$ keeps growing without bound as $x\rightarrow\infty$, while $\frac{1}{x^2}$'s faster decay allows its total area to converge.
questions.explanation: Both curves decrease, but $\frac{1}{x}$ stays larger than $\frac{1}{x^2}$ for all $x>1$ (e.g. at $x=10$: $0.1$ vs $0.01$). This slower decay means the accumulated area under $\frac{1}{x}$ keeps growing without bound as $x\rightarrow\infty$, while $\frac{1}{x^2}$'s faster decay allows its total area to converge.

questions.q: Set up (but do not solve for constants) the partial fraction decomposition of $\frac{3x^2+2}{(x-1)(x^2+4)}$.
questions.target: Partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic factor
questions.answer: Since $x^2+4$ is irreducible over the reals, the decomposition has the form $\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}$.

questions.q: State the p-test for $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$, and use it to determine convergence for $p=3$ and $p=0.5$.
questions.answer: $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converges if $p>1$ and diverges if $p\leq1$. For $p=3>1$: converges. For $p=0.5\leq1$: diverges.
questions.explanation: $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converges if $p>1$ and diverges if $p\leq1$. For $p=3>1$: converges. For $p=0.5\leq1$: diverges.

questions.q: State the analogous p-test for $\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ (a discontinuity at $x=0$), and determine convergence for $p=\frac{1}{2}$ and $p=2$.
questions.cross_lesson: 5.01 Sequences and Basic Series Convergence Tests
questions.answer: $\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converges if $p<1$ and diverges if $p\geq1$ (opposite condition from the infinite-limit case). For $p=\frac{1}{2}<1$: converges. For $p=2\geq1$: diverges.
questions.explanation: $\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converges if $p<1$ and diverges if $p\geq1$ (opposite condition from the infinite-limit case). For $p=\frac{1}{2}<1$: converges. For $p=2\geq1$: diverges.

questions.target: Combining partial fractions with improper integrals
questions.cross_lesson: 5.02 Ratio, Root, and Alternating Series Tests
questions.answer: $\frac{1}{(x+1)(x+2)}=\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}$. $\int_0^{b}\left(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}\right)dx=\left[\ln\frac{x+1}{x+2}\right]_0^b=\ln\frac{b+1}{b+2}-\ln\frac{1}{2}$. As $b\rightarrow\infty$, $\frac{b+1}{b+2}\rightarrow1$, so the limit is $\ln1-\ln\frac{1}{2}=\ln2$. Converges to $\ln2$.
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{(x+1)(x+2)}=\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}$. $\int_0^{b}\left(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}\right)dx=\left[\ln\frac{x+1}{x+2}\right]_0^b=\ln\frac{b+1}{b+2}-\ln\frac{1}{2}$. As $b\rightarrow\infty$, $\frac{b+1}{b+2}\rightarrow1$, so the limit is $\ln1-\ln\frac{1}{2}=\ln2$. Converges to $\ln2$.

questions.cross_lesson: 6.01 Power Series and Interval of Convergence
questions.answer: $\frac{6x^2-3x-1}{x(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-1}+\frac{C}{x+1}$. $6x^2-3x-1=A(x-1)(x+1)+Bx(x+1)+Cx(x-1)$. At $x=0$: $-1=-A \Rightarrow A=1$. At $x=1$: $2=2B \Rightarrow B=1$. At $x=-1$: $8=2C \Rightarrow C=4$. So $\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{4}{x+1}$.
questions.explanation: $\frac{6x^2-3x-1}{x(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-1}+\frac{C}{x+1}$. $6x^2-3x-1=A(x-1)(x+1)+Bx(x+1)+Cx(x-1)$. At $x=0$: $-1=-A \Rightarrow A=1$. At $x=1$: $2=2B \Rightarrow B=1$. At $x=-1$: $8=2C \Rightarrow C=4$. So $\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{4}{x+1}$.

questions.q: The convergent improper integral $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx=1$ (shown earlier) means the infinite region under $y=\frac{1}{x^2}$ for $x\geq1$ has FINITE area. Explain intuitively why this is possible even though the region extends forever.
questions.target: Visualizing convergence: area under the curve
questions.answer: Even though the region is infinitely long, the height $\frac{1}{x^2}$ shrinks fast enough as $x\rightarrow\infty$ that the accumulated area still converges to a finite total — the 'tail' contributes less and less area, summing to a bounded amount, similar to how a convergent geometric series sums to a finite value despite infinitely many terms.
questions.explanation: Even though the region is infinitely long, the height $\frac{1}{x^2}$ shrinks fast enough as $x\rightarrow\infty$ that the accumulated area still converges to a finite total — the 'tail' contributes less and less area, summing to a bounded amount, similar to how a convergent geometric series sums to a finite value despite infinitely many terms.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^1\frac{2}{x^{\frac{1}{4}}}\,dx$, or show it diverges (the integrand is undefined at $x=0$).
questions.answer: Since $p=\frac{1}{4}<1$, this converges (by the $p$-test at a discontinuity). $\int_0^12x^{-\frac{1}{4}}\,dx=\lim_{a\rightarrow0^+}\left[\frac{2x^{\frac{3}{4}}}{\frac{3}{4}}\right]_a^1=\frac{2}{\frac{3}{4}}-0=\frac{8}{3}$.
questions.explanation: Since $p=\frac{1}{4}<1$, this converges (by the $p$-test at a discontinuity). $\int_0^12x^{-\frac{1}{4}}\,dx=\lim_{a\rightarrow0^+}\left[\frac{2x^{\frac{3}{4}}}{\frac{3}{4}}\right]_a^1=\frac{2}{\frac{3}{4}}-0=\frac{8}{3}$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^1\frac{6}{x^{\frac{1}{5}}}\,dx$, or show it diverges (the integrand is undefined at $x=0$).
questions.target: Partial fraction decomposition: distinct linear factors
questions.answer: Since $p=\frac{1}{5}<1$, this converges (by the $p$-test at a discontinuity). $\int_0^16x^{-\frac{1}{5}}\,dx=\lim_{a\rightarrow0^+}\left[\frac{6x^{\frac{4}{5}}}{\frac{4}{5}}\right]_a^1=\frac{6}{\frac{4}{5}}-0=\frac{15}{2}$.
questions.explanation: Since $p=\frac{1}{5}<1$, this converges (by the $p$-test at a discontinuity). $\int_0^16x^{-\frac{1}{5}}\,dx=\lim_{a\rightarrow0^+}\left[\frac{6x^{\frac{4}{5}}}{\frac{4}{5}}\right]_a^1=\frac{6}{\frac{4}{5}}-0=\frac{15}{2}$.

questions.q: Use a direct comparison to determine whether $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{2+\sin x}{x^2}\,dx$ converges or diverges.
choices: Cannot be determined by comparison, since $\sin x$ oscillates.
Diverges, since $\frac{2+\sin x}{x^2}\geq\frac{1}{x^2}$ for $x\geq1$, and $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ diverges since $p=2\leq1$.
Converges, since $\frac{2+\sin x}{x^2}\leq\frac{3}{x^2}$ for $x\geq1$, and $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{3}{x^2}\,dx$ converges since $p=2>1$.
Converges only because $a=2$ happens to be even.
questions.answer: Since $-1\leq\sin x\leq1$: Converges, since $\frac{2+\sin x}{x^2}\leq\frac{3}{x^2}$ for $x\geq1$, and $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{3}{x^2}\,dx$ converges since $p=2>1$.
questions.explanation: Since $-1\leq\sin x\leq1$: Converges, since $\frac{2+\sin x}{x^2}\leq\frac{3}{x^2}$ for $x\geq1$, and $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{3}{x^2}\,dx$ converges since $p=2>1$.

questions.q: Use a direct comparison to determine whether $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{5+\sin x}{x}\,dx$ converges or diverges.
choices: Diverges only because $a=5$ happens to be even.
Diverges, since $\frac{5+\sin x}{x}\geq\frac{4}{x}$ for $x\geq1$, and $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{4}{x}\,dx$ diverges since $p=1\leq1$.
Cannot be determined by comparison, since $\sin x$ oscillates.
Converges, since $\frac{5+\sin x}{x}\leq\frac{6}{x}$ for $x\geq1$, and $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{6}{x}\,dx$ converges since $p=1>1$.
questions.answer: Since $-1\leq\sin x\leq1$: Diverges, since $\frac{5+\sin x}{x}\geq\frac{4}{x}$ for $x\geq1$, and $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{4}{x}\,dx$ diverges since $p=1\leq1$.
questions.explanation: Since $-1\leq\sin x\leq1$: Diverges, since $\frac{5+\sin x}{x}\geq\frac{4}{x}$ for $x\geq1$, and $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{4}{x}\,dx$ diverges since $p=1\leq1$.

questions.q: When must long division be performed BEFORE applying partial fractions?
choices: When the degree of the numerator is greater than or equal to the degree of the denominator
When the denominator has repeated roots
When the numerator is a constant
questions.answer: Partial fractions applies only to proper rational functions. If $\deg(P) \geq \deg(Q)$, polynomial long division must be performed first.
questions.explanation: Partial fractions applies only to proper rational functions. If $\deg(P) \geq \deg(Q)$, polynomial long division must be performed first.

questions.q: For what values of $p$ does the improper integral $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^p} dx$ converge?
questions.answer: By the $p$-integral test, $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^p} dx$ converges if and only if $p > 1$ (to $\frac{1}{p - 1}$), and diverges for $p \leq 1$.
questions.explanation: By the $p$-integral test, $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^p} dx$ converges if and only if $p > 1$ (to $\frac{1}{p - 1}$), and diverges for $p \leq 1$.

questions.answer: The integrand has an infinite discontinuity at $x = 0$: $\lim_{a \rightarrow 0^+} [2\sqrt{x}]_a^1 = 2(1) - 0 = 2$.
questions.explanation: The integrand has an infinite discontinuity at $x = 0$: $\lim_{a \rightarrow 0^+} [2\sqrt{x}]_a^1 = 2(1) - 0 = 2$.
